title: Not a record collector; live playing versus records
summary: Royal never kept records, prefers live audience interaction, and calls records a poor imitation of performance.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Critics, polls and the jazz press

blocks.x: So, you've never made any kind of effort to keep track of all the records (inaudible)?

No, not really. I'm not a record collector. I never have collected records. I just never worried about it. Traveling on the road for 20 years with Basie, I couldn't be carrying records around with me.

And that was probably the -- some of the most progressive type of my life, through continued stage, was that 20 years, doing the same thing that I was tied into. So, during that time, I didn't collect any records. So, there --

Yeah, I have some of those records that were given to me by the recording company and sent to my house and some of them still have the jackets on them, had the jackets on them for the last 15 years, never played.
Oh, that's too bad. (Inaudible) you're not interested in them (inaudible).

Sometimes, yes. I like the feeling of playing in person, where you get the pulsations from live audiences and people that are actually enjoying themselves. That's when I enjoy playing music and it's great gratification sometimes to have people that idolize you and give honest applause and keep you going. That's part of the beauty of
Do you feel that there is an exchange between the musicians in the audience --

There's -- definitely. There's charisma interchangeable on both sides. You can make love with your horn. You can look out in the audience and charm somebody if you really get the right person that wants to be charmed. You can turn people on with your horn. You can turn people off with your horn if you want to, if you know how. So, it's a lot of fun when you're doing it in person and the mechanical being of it is wonderful for making money, but the mechanical making of a record is pure trash, in my estimation, because the real thing is the performance itself, because that's what the record is actually trying to reproduce, is the pure performance, which they very, very seldom achieve.
